tagline: Low on air, high on life.

home.heroTitle: Architect by profession. Adventurer by instinct.
home.heroSubtitle: I spend my professional life solving complex problems and my personal life looking for harder ones.
home.professionalSubtitle: Enterprise Technical Architecture Director, focused on end-to-end enterprise architecture for global organizations.
home.personalSubtitle: PADI Divemaster, mountaineer, skier and traveler, 58 of 195 countries and counting.
home.quote: Every step before this one led me here. I could never have imagined how fortunate I would be to experience all of this and meet so many interesting people along the way. Every step, every breath, every experience has shaped me and let me think bigger than ever before, always seeking what this beautiful world has to give.
home.calloutMountaineerLine: One deliberate step at a time.
home.closingQuote: Stay curious enough to wonder what's possible, resilient enough to keep going when it isn't easy, and brave enough to find out. There is too much life to experience, too much world to explore, and too much within me yet to discover.

about.accentLine: Architect by profession. Adventurer by instinct.
about.locationLine: A global citizen, always on the move across time zones.
about.p1: For more than a decade, I have been helping global organisations solve complex business challenges through technology. My career has been built at the intersection of enterprise architecture, strategic consulting, and hands-on engineering, transforming ambitious business objectives into scalable, practical solutions that deliver measurable value.
about.p2: As an <1>Enterprise Technical Architecture Director</1>, I partner with executives, business leaders, and delivery teams to design enterprise-scale digital transformation programs, with a focus on end-to-end enterprise architecture. My expertise spans Salesforce architecture, Quote-to-Cash, Revenue Lifecycle Management, CRM strategy, system integration, cloud platforms, and enterprise solution design across industries including Financial Services, Telecommunications, Manufacturing, SaaS, Analytics, and Professional Services.
about.p3: I believe great architecture is never just about technology. It's about understanding people, aligning stakeholders, simplifying complexity, and creating systems that remain adaptable for years to come.
about.journey: I consider myself a global citizen. I've lived and worked in Silicon Valley, California; London, UK; Zurich, Switzerland; San Francisco, California; and Melbourne, Australia, calling several countries home along the way. Each move meant starting a new life from scratch in a new country, which has made me highly adaptable and resilient, and given me a natural ease connecting with people from any background.
about.leadIntro: The way I lead has been shaped just as much outside the office as inside it.
about.divemaster: As a <1>PADI Divemaster</1>, I've learned that preparation, calm decision-making, and trust are essential when leading people in challenging environments. Overcoming fear starts in your head, and you simply never give up.
about.mountaineer: As a <1>mountaineer</1>, I've experienced that meaningful achievements are built one deliberate step at a time. Success comes from resilience, planning, and adapting when conditions inevitably change, because everything is in your head: you face your fears and never give up.
about.marathon: As a <1>marathon runner</1>, I've learned that consistency outperforms intensity. Long-term results come from discipline, persistence, and continuous improvement rather than quick wins. It's proof that everything is in your head: overcome the fear, and never give up.
about.continents: Having <1>lived and worked across three continents</1>, I've developed a global perspective that allows me to collaborate effectively with diverse teams, understand different business cultures, and build strong relationships across organisations.
about.closing: Because the best solutions don't simply solve today's problems. They create opportunities for tomorrow.
about.hook: I have always been drawn to the edge of the familiar.
about.professional: Professionally, that means solving complex problems, designing enterprise architectures, and leading people through ambiguity. Fifteen years in, I have learned to turn complexity into clarity, ideas into solutions, and challenges into possibilities.
about.personal: Beyond technology, I seek a different kind of terrain: mountains, oceans, snow, unfamiliar places. As a PADI Divemaster, mountaineer, skier, climber and explorer, I have learned that resilience is built one difficult step at a time, that courage rarely means having no fear, and that the best views are usually earned.
about.explore: To explore. To understand. To push beyond what I thought was possible.
about.horizon: And to keep moving toward whatever lies beyond the horizon.

leadership.title: Calm decisions, made under real pressure
leadership.subtitle: How the same instincts that hold up on a rock face or a dive show up in how I lead teams.
leadership.p1: Great architecture is never just about technology. It's about understanding people, aligning stakeholders, simplifying complexity, and creating systems that remain adaptable for years to come.
leadership.p2: In my current role, I lead critical program components end to end: client negotiations, SOW development, executive steering committees, and project governance, while orchestrating global, multi-regional programs across both waterfall and agile delivery.
leadership.quote: Preparation, calm decision-making, and trust are essential when leading people in challenging environments.
leadership.teamText: I manage a team of 10 direct reports, and mentor Solution and Technical Architects as well as delivery teams of up to 80 people, building consulting capability and technical depth across the organization.
leadership.programsText: I've led multiple pro bono AI for Good initiatives, deploying Agentforce and Data Cloud solutions to expand educational access for students from underinvested communities.

dead-woman-s-pass-inca-trail.title: Dead Woman's Pass, Inca Trail
dead-woman-s-pass-inca-trail.why: The classic high point of the Inca Trail, and my first taste of trekking to altitude on foot rather than by car or cable car.
dead-woman-s-pass-inca-trail.challenge: The steep, humid ascent tested my legs and lungs more than the altitude itself, over 1,000 stone steps with no technical climbing to break up the grind.
dead-woman-s-pass-inca-trail.moment: Reaching the pass and looking back down the valley at the trail winding through the cloud forest below.
dead-woman-s-pass-inca-trail.lesson: Altitude discomfort is manageable with a steady pace, even without any technical mountaineering skills.

the-lost-city.title: The Lost City
the-lost-city.why: A multi-day jungle trek to a pre-Columbian ruin, chosen for the mix of culture and physical challenge.
the-lost-city.challenge: The relentless heat and humidity across rolling, steep terrain made this more draining than the modest elevation would suggest.
the-lost-city.moment: Climbing the final stone steps into the ruins after days of jungle trekking.
the-lost-city.lesson: Heat and humidity can be a bigger limiting factor than elevation or technical difficulty.

root-glacier-wrangell-st-elias-national-.title: Root Glacier, Wrangell, St. Elias National Park and Preserve
root-glacier-wrangell-st-elias-national-.why: My first real introduction to glacier travel and ice climbing, in one of the largest icefields in North America.
root-glacier-wrangell-st-elias-national-.challenge: Learning to trust crampons and an ice axe on glacial ice, with crevasses adding real consequence to every step.
root-glacier-wrangell-st-elias-national-.moment: Standing on blue glacial ice deep inside Wrangell-St. Elias, a landscape unlike anything I'd trekked before.
root-glacier-wrangell-st-elias-national-.lesson: Ice climbing and crevasse awareness are foundational skills worth building early, before attempting bigger glaciated peaks.

mt-shasta-helen-lake-2022.title: Mt. Shasta
mt-shasta-helen-lake-2022.subtitle: Helen Lake
mt-shasta-helen-lake-2022.why: A training climb to build glacier travel and crampon skills ahead of bigger objectives.
mt-shasta-helen-lake-2022.challenge: Conditions on the day turned us back below Helen Lake, a reminder that summits are optional and safety isn't.
mt-shasta-helen-lake-2022.moment: Practicing self-arrest and crampon technique on the snowfield below the summit.
mt-shasta-helen-lake-2022.lesson: Turning around before the summit is still a successful climb if it keeps the team safe.

mt-whitney-2022.title: Mt. Whitney
mt-whitney-2022.why: The tallest peak in the contiguous US, and a natural next step after Shasta to test endurance at altitude.
mt-whitney-2022.challenge: A long, non-technical push where fitness and pacing mattered more than any single technical move.
mt-whitney-2022.moment: Handling the altitude comfortably even as the day stretched long.
mt-whitney-2022.lesson: Endurance and pacing carry a climb just as much as technical skill does.

half-dome-2022.title: Half Dome
half-dome-2022.why: An iconic Yosemite day hike, capped by the exposed cable route to the summit.
half-dome-2022.challenge: The final cable-assisted pitch up the granite dome demanded steady nerves rather than technical gear.
half-dome-2022.moment: Topping out on Half Dome with Yosemite Valley spread out below.
half-dome-2022.lesson: Exposure, not elevation or technical grade, is sometimes the real test of a climb.

mt-kilimanjaro.title: Mt. Kilimanjaro
mt-kilimanjaro.why: The highest peak in Africa, and my first multi-day expedition-style climb above 5,000 meters.
mt-kilimanjaro.challenge: Six days of steady altitude gain, with the final steep push to Uhuru Peak testing endurance in the thin air.
mt-kilimanjaro.moment: Watching the sunrise from the summit after a night push through the steep scree to the crater rim.
mt-kilimanjaro.lesson: Slow, steady acclimatization over multiple days pays off more than raw fitness alone.

mt-everest-base-camp.title: Mt. Everest Base Camp
mt-everest-base-camp.why: A trek to the foot of the world's highest mountain, through the Khumbu valley and its Sherpa villages.
mt-everest-base-camp.challenge: Ten days of cumulative altitude gain and -15 C nights, with steep trail sections testing stamina daily.
mt-everest-base-camp.moment: Standing at Base Camp with the Khumbu Icefall rising above, Everest itself finally in view.
mt-everest-base-camp.lesson: Multi-day altitude treks reward patience; the body needs time, not force, to adapt.

kala-patthar.title: Kala Patthar
kala-patthar.why: The highest point of the Everest Base Camp trek, climbed the day after reaching Base Camp for the best view of Everest itself.
kala-patthar.challenge: The highest altitude I'd reached to date, on a steep pre-dawn climb in the cold.
kala-patthar.moment: Watching sunrise light hit Everest's summit from Kala Patthar's viewpoint.
kala-patthar.lesson: The extra push beyond Base Camp is worth it for the perspective it gives on the whole range.

mt-shasta-helen-lake-2023.title: Mt. Shasta
mt-shasta-helen-lake-2023.subtitle: Helen Lake
mt-shasta-helen-lake-2023.why: A return to Shasta to train in rope team travel and crevasse rescue, skills the earlier attempt didn't require.
mt-shasta-helen-lake-2023.challenge: Weather again kept us off the summit, but the technical training was the real objective of the climb.
mt-shasta-helen-lake-2023.moment: Practicing avalanche and crevasse rescue drills as a rope team on the mountain itself, not in a classroom.
mt-shasta-helen-lake-2023.lesson: Rescue skills are only real once they're practiced under actual mountain conditions.

mt-whitney-2023.title: Mt. Whitney
mt-whitney-2023.why: A second attempt on Whitney, this time via a steeper, more technical route to build on the previous training climbs.
mt-whitney-2023.challenge: Steep snow and lingering avalanche risk turned the team back short of the summit.
mt-whitney-2023.moment: Running avalanche rescue drills on Whitney's slopes as part of the climb itself.
mt-whitney-2023.lesson: Not every technical climb needs to end at the summit to be worth doing.

mt-rainier-muir-camp-no-summit-condition.title: Mt. Rainier
mt-rainier-muir-camp-no-summit-condition.subtitle: Camp Muir, no summit conditions
mt-rainier-muir-camp-no-summit-condition.why: A glaciated volcano climbed with a friend to build rope work and knot skills ahead of bigger objectives like Aconcagua.
mt-rainier-muir-camp-no-summit-condition.challenge: We stopped at Camp Muir rather than pushing for the summit, with -10 C temperatures and steep glacier travel testing the rope team.
mt-rainier-muir-camp-no-summit-condition.moment: Tying climbing knots and practicing self-arrest on Rainier's glacier with a close friend by my side.
mt-rainier-muir-camp-no-summit-condition.lesson: Building technical skill with the right partner matters more than chasing every summit.

aconcagua.title: Aconcagua
aconcagua.why: The highest peak outside Asia, and the biggest test yet of everything built up through the training climbs on Shasta, Whitney, and Rainier.
aconcagua.challenge: Two and a half weeks at altitude, -30 C temperatures on summit day, and a team that was whittled down to just 3 of 12 by the top.
aconcagua.moment: Standing on the summit of the Americas' highest peak, one of only three from the group who made it.
aconcagua.lesson: On big mountains, the mountain and the weather decide who summits, not just fitness or determination.

mt-baker.title: Mt. Baker
mt-baker.why: A heavily glaciated Cascades volcano, and a chance to put Aconcagua-honed rope and rescue skills to full use.
mt-baker.challenge: Navigating crevasse fields as a rope team in -15 C temperatures, with the full toolkit of knots and rescue technique in play.
mt-baker.moment: Reaching the summit as part of a well-organized rope team after two days of technical glacier travel.
mt-baker.lesson: The steady accumulation of technical skills across smaller climbs makes bigger glaciated peaks feel achievable.

half-dome-2024.title: Half Dome
half-dome-2024.why: A return to a familiar trail, this time solo, to test self-reliance on a climb I'd already done with others.
half-dome-2024.challenge: Managing pacing, navigation, and decision-making entirely on my own, with no one else to share the load.
half-dome-2024.moment: Standing on the summit alone, having made every call on the mountain myself.
half-dome-2024.lesson: Soloing a known route builds a different kind of confidence than doing it with a group.

mt-whitney-2024.title: Mt. Whitney
mt-whitney-2024.why: A late-season solo return to finally summit Whitney, after two earlier attempts were turned back by conditions.
mt-whitney-2024.challenge: Camping alone through a -25 C night before a steep, crampon-dependent push to the top.
mt-whitney-2024.moment: Finally reaching Whitney's summit solo, after two prior attempts had ended short of the top.
mt-whitney-2024.lesson: Persistence across multiple attempts, and the willingness to go back alone, is what closes out a summit.

mt-shasta.title: Mt. Shasta
mt-shasta.why: A third attempt on Shasta, this time solo, to finally close out a peak that had turned me back twice before.
mt-shasta.challenge: A grueling 16-hour push through the night and into the day, alone, on very steep terrain.
mt-shasta.moment: Topping out on Shasta after 16 hours on the mountain, the third time being the charm.
mt-shasta.lesson: Some summits take multiple attempts, and the solo attempt is often the one that finally works.

breithorn.title: Breithorn
breithorn.why: A Swiss 4000er climbed as a warm-up and acclimatization step ahead of Mont Blanc two days later.
breithorn.challenge: Roped glacier travel in a 2x3 team, with steep sections requiring careful crampon work.
breithorn.moment: Summiting my first Alpine 4000-meter peak, with the Mont Blanc massif visible in the distance.
breithorn.lesson: A shorter acclimatization climb right before a bigger objective makes the harder day that follows more manageable.

mont-blanc-via-trois-monts.title: Mont Blanc via Trois Monts
mont-blanc-via-trois-monts.why: The highest peak in the Alps, and the culmination of years of building glacier and rope skills on Rainier, Baker, and Aconcagua.
mont-blanc-via-trois-monts.challenge: A 16-hour summit day jumping crevasses, climbing a near-vertical wall on all fours, and roped travel across exposed terrain the whole way.
mont-blanc-via-trois-monts.moment: Standing on the roof of Western Europe after the most technically demanding day of climbing I'd done to date.
mont-blanc-via-trois-monts.lesson: The hardest climbs are where every previously learned skill, rope work, crevasse crossing, endurance, all get used at once.

mount-kosciuszko.title: Mount Kosciuszko
mount-kosciuszko.why: The highest peak on the Australian mainland, and a chance to add a seventh continent high point to the list.
mount-kosciuszko.challenge: Cold, gusty winds on an otherwise non-technical trail made for a bracing rather than a difficult climb.
mount-kosciuszko.moment: Summiting Kosciuszko into strong wind gusts, a stark contrast to the glaciated giants climbed before it.
mount-kosciuszko.lesson: Not every summit needs to be technical to be worth doing, sometimes the wind and cold are the whole story.
